what_changed: app/works.py type-checks the candidate slot so a studio, a piece of leader, a costume cluster or a restatement of the input cannot be scored as an identity.
The identity gate gained competing_hypotheses>=2 and leading_hypothesis_least_contradicted, from Heuer's Analysis of Competing Hypotheses. Seven thresholds became nine.
The Skeptic is asked to find a rival identity rather than only attack the incumbent, and the compiler is told a lone candidate will not pass.
honest_reading: One defect was fixed and the other was not, and the second result is the more interesting one. Candidates that named no film went from 7 in 19 runs to 0 in 9 -- but that is true by construction, since the type check removes them, so it is evidence the filter runs, not evidence the system reasons better. False-confident identifications did NOT improve: 5 of 19 runs before (26%), 4 of 9 after (44%). At these sample sizes that difference is indistinguishable from noise in either direction, and no rate should be quoted from it.

what_actually_happened: The type check converted disguised failures into visible ones. Before the fix, when the pipeline had no real answer it filled the candidate slot with something that was not a film -- a studio, a costume period, a restatement of the input -- and that scored as 'malformed', neither right nor wrong. With non-films rejected, the compiler still produces something, and now it produces an actual film title, which is usually the wrong one. D04 no longer returns 'Un coin de Paris' three times running; it returns 'Champs Elysees (1900)' once and abstains once. Different wrong answer, same underlying problem. The candidate slot was acting as a pressure valve, and constraining its type changed what came out of it rather than closing it.
what_this_implies: The measured error rate was always roughly this high. The malformed candidates were hiding it, which means the pre-fix figures published at /v1/eval/stability flattered the system more than we realised at the time. Whether a visible wrong film is better or worse than an obvious non-answer is a real question: it is more honest and more dangerous. It is more dangerous because an archivist can act on it, which is exactly why the gate still refuses to assert it.
caveats: n = 9 runs after the fix, across 5 fragments. This shows direction at best.

`cases_with_a_stable_verdict` reads 3 of 5 after the fix, up from 1 of 5, but two of those cases have only one recorded run each and are therefore trivially 'stable'. The figure is a measurement artifact of the smaller era and should not be quoted.
One run in the after era returned HTTP 502 and is recorded as a delivery failure, not as a verdict.
what_did_hold: Across all 28 recorded runs in both eras, no run ever reached `probable`. Every wrong answer above, before and after, was returned as `candidates` with its failing thresholds attached. That is the property the architecture actually guarantees, and it is the only one that has survived every measurement taken.
next_thing_to_try: Make 'no candidate' a first-class output the compiler is asked for explicitly, rather than an absence it falls into. The type check tells the model what a candidate may not be; nothing yet tells it that returning none is a correct and expected outcome.
